title: Training Data: Teach the Robot Yourself
description: Label a set of pictures yourself and watch the exact problem every learned model has, happen in your own hands.

content.value: A model doesn't learn from instructions — it learns from labelled examples: here's a picture, here's what it is. Enough examples, and it can start guessing correctly on pictures it's never seen before. You're about to do the labelling yourself.

content.title: 🏷️ Label them all
content.hint: Tag every card as cat or dog, then test the result on a new one.

content.value: Notice the model's guess on the final image is only ever as good as what it was shown. If every training example was a very typical, clear cat or dog, an unusual example — a wolf, a blurry photo, an odd breed — can genuinely fool it, not because the underlying idea is broken, but because that particular shape of example was never part of what it learned from.

This is the single most important idea in this whole module: data quality and coverage is the real work behind any learned system. More or better examples, covering more of the situations a robot will actually meet, matters more than almost anything else.

This connects directly back to Module 7's line-following. A rule you wrote by hand handles exactly the cases you thought of. A trained model handles exactly the cases it was trained on. Neither approach magically covers cases nobody prepared it for.

Key takeaway: a model learns entirely from its training examples. A gap between what it was trained on and what it actually encounters is where mistakes come from — which is why data quality, not just clever programming, is the real work behind a learned system.

quiz.question: What does a model actually learn from, according to this lesson?
options: A list of instructions written by a programmer
Labelled examples — pictures paired with what they actually are
quiz.explain: Learning from examples, not instructions, is the defining difference between a learned and a rule-based approach.

quiz.question: Why can an unusual image (like the wolf) fool a model trained only on clear cat and dog photos?
options: The underlying idea is fundamentally broken
That particular kind of example was never part of what the model was shown, so it has no learned pattern to match it against
Models can never be trained to recognise animals
quiz.explain: A model's guesses are bounded by what it actually saw during training — an unfamiliar shape of example is exactly where it's likely to fail.

quiz.question: What's the single most important factor behind a well-performing learned system, according to this lesson?
options: Data quality and coverage of the training examples
How fast the computer running it is
How many lines of code the programmer wrote
quiz.explain: Good, representative training data is what this whole lesson is built around — arguably more important than the algorithm itself.
